item.title: Deceivers Come in Three Main Types
item.description:
Deception

Deceivers Come in Three Main Types

If love is a battlefield, not everyone fights fair.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Deception is common in romantic relationships, but not everyone deceives for the same reasons.
  • New research sorts individuals into deception types and reveals shared motivational patterns.
  • Antagonistic Strategists might be rare, but they regularly deceive their partners.
  • The healthiest type is aligned with relationship security and satisfaction.

Romantic relationships are home to some of our most honest, truthful moments. We speak authentically, we confess, we lay it all on the table. Unfortunately, they’re also the context for some of our most devious, deceptive acts. From little omissions to egregious betrayals, romantic partners—at least many of us—know very well how to deceive.

Why People Deceive Their Romantic Partners

Deception is strategic. People try to cover up their mistakes; they try to make themselves appear in a more positive light; they hide their real feelings or thoughts and pretend their misbehaviors never happened; they try to avoid a conflict.

Some of these motives are pro-relational. Why start a fight? It’s a minor thing. The truth would probably cause more harm than good. Better to say, “I loved that concert. I can see why he’s your favorite artist,” than to spoil the night. And it benefits no one to know that you went to the restroom to spit out your partner’s disgusting pie. Nor does it make the world right to tell your partner you’re home late because you stopped by your buddy’s place: traffic is a ready excuse.

Other times, deceptions are malicious or self-serving. Misleading a partner so that you get the win or ruin their plans; making up information to sound more interesting and keep a partner’s attention. These motives are clearly different than the pro-relational motives that drive others.

Patterns Tied to People, Not Deceptive Acts

Any one act of deception (e.g., lying) could be motivated by kindness or cruelty, so it’s unlikely that specific acts of deception are linked to certain motives. Instead, people might bring a tendency toward a certain type of deception into their relationship. The question becomes: What kinds of people hold certain motives for deception?

Recent research explored this topic by surveying 567 people in the United States, about half women, half men, all of whom reported being currently in a romantic relationship (Cole and Stonebrook, 2026). Participants completed a series of measures, including an assessment of motivations for deception, and then the researchers applied latent profile analysis (LPA) to see if people naturally clustered into different groups based on their typical motivations.

Three Main Types of Deceivers

Analyses revealed three primary types of deceivers (Cole and Stonebrook, 2026). Think about yourself (or your romantic partner!). Which best describes you?

  1. Strategic Soothers: “Don’t make waves” is the motto for this group. Strategic soothers want to avoid conflict, conceal mistakes, and are low in malicious intent. They’re not catering to a partner’s emotions to get attention; they do it to keep the peace. Just shy of half of participants (48 percent) fell into this category.
  2. Transparent Partners: Well, hello partners who don’t deceive! Compared to the other clusters, participants sorted into this category (38 percent) were higher in attachment security and low on all motives to deceive. Interestingly, this bunch also reported the highest relationship satisfaction. Honesty, it appears, is the best policy.
  3. Antagonistic Strategists: People in this category are not afraid of deception. They engage in it often, and for a wide variety of reasons, including malicious motives. About 15 percent of the sample fell into this group. In general, individuals in this category were higher in narcissism, psychopathy, and sadism compared to people in the other categories. They also reported lower relationship satisfaction.

Transparency for the Win

Deception may happen in relationships, but not everyone has the same reasons, and some people are more apt to engage in it than others (Cole and Stonebrook, 2026). This research shows that a particular type of partner, the Antagonistic Strategist, makes deception a part of their relationship maintenance playbook. These individuals have few constraints on their deception and are ready to use it, particularly if it can help them exert their own control.

Meanwhile, Strategic Soothers are struggling. They have attachment insecurities like Antagonistic Strategists but manage them quite differently. They want to keep dynamics steady and are particularly apt to use deception so that they can avoid conflict and appease their partners.

The Transparent Partners take a different approach. Their low drive for deception, coupled with their relational security and satisfaction, suggests that open communication is, indeed, a helpful strategy. The low use of deception suggests honesty is the primary tool for navigating situations that are uncertain, missteps, or other challenges.

What is not known from this research is whether happy couples, like those in the Transparent Partners group, are simply not encountering situations that might open the door to deception. In other words, maybe people high in attachment security create patterns in their relationships for which deception is not possible. Future research might lean into the question of opportunity versus strategy when it comes to differences in the use of deception.

item.title: That Thing That Wasn’t Your Fault: Healing a Lifelong Wound
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

That Thing That Wasn’t Your Fault: Healing a Lifelong Wound

Life can blossom dramatically when you have the courage to confront old wounds.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly all schools of psychoanalysis are based on this: if you would be healed, turn and face your wounds.
  • The hard truth of truly healing from an old wound is that it requires the willingness to go back and feel it.
  • The courage to face old wounds or traumas invites a heartbreakthrough—a heartbreak and a breakthrough.

The most famous scene in the movie Good Will Hunting is the “It’s not your fault” scene.

Will Hunting, played by Matt Damon, is a genius whose intellect is largely stuck inside him, along with his ability to love. After several months of counseling with a psychologist played by Robin Williams (it’s either therapy or jail, for assaulting a cop), it becomes clear that what’s holding Will back is the fact that he had an abusive childhood—a foster father who regularly beat him.

“You know, it’s not your fault,” the psychologist tells Will.

“I know,” Will says with a shrug.

“Look at me, son. It’s not your fault”

“Yeah. I know.”

“No, you don’t. It’s not your fault.”

Will just stares at him.

“It’s not your fault,” the psychologist says again.

“Don’t f--- with me.”

“It’s not your fault.”

“Don’t f--- with me. Not you.”

“It’s not your fault.”

Finally, Will buries his head in his hands and bursts into tears, along with—if memory serves me—much of the audience, myself included.

Apparently, many of us have experienced something that wasn’t our fault, but we’ve been hauling around with us our whole life as if it was. Likely something our parents did or didn’t do, or something we believe we did or didn’t do that made them stop approving of us or withdraw their love, that made us afraid to be ourselves and trust the world.

Whatever those original wounds were—abuse, betrayal, abandonment, rejection, shame, neglect—they ended up playing a starring role in who we turned out to be and how our lives unfolded, whether we’re aware of it or not. The kind of partners we continually attract, the dramas we keep reenacting with those partners, the stories we tell about ourselves and the world, the dreams that keep coming back, the ways we self-sabotage, even the kind of work we end up doing.

But the movie also portrays—true to life, in my experience—that Will blossoms dramatically after this confrontation with his childhood wound, coming into his power, his gift, and his heart.

But the cold truth of healing from a wound like this is that you’ve got to be willing to feel the thing. To go back and touch it, re-encounter the grief of it, starting with the brute fact that you got a bum deal, that justice is beside the point, and no one’s going to make it up to you, and maybe the best you can do is retell the story of your life with the wound as the middle of the story, not the end.

Now I don’t want to oversell the value of such a confrontation with the past. It’s certainly not for everybody, and you can have a perfectly satisfactory life without facing off with your demons. A very successful and high-functioning relative of mine recently described the “psychological uncoupling that allows me to put childhood difficulties behind me, and be relieved not to think about them anymore.”

Psychological uncoupling might sound like another word for denial, but denial isn’t always a bad thing. Perhaps my relative’s coping strategy is just a more protracted version of the kind of healthy denial you might employ to keep anxiety at bay long enough to deliver a speech.

Still, not thinking about old wounds anymore may be a relief, but it isn’t the same as healing from them, though it’s arguable which takes more effort. Squaring off with old wounds or traumas is no picnic, but neither is the constant vigilance and self-monitoring required to avoid thinking about them. Despite your best-laid plans, the ghost of that thing that wasn’t your fault can readily mutate into emotional numbness, self-defeating patterns, mental-health struggles, and possibly ill health.

And because you often encounter such symptoms far downstream from whatever set them in motion, you may have to swim back upstream to the source in order to properly treat them, rather than trying to ignore or medicate them into oblivion because you don’t want to “dig up the past, open a can of worms, rock the boat.” Even if that way lies healing. My mother once captured this philosophy of avoidance when she said of an old anguish, “If I start crying, I’ll never stop, and I’ll flood the basement.”

The truth is you do stop crying, and the willingness to give in to it is a heartbreakthrough—a heartbreak and a breakthrough.

In fact, nearly all schools of psychoanalytic thought are based on this: if you would be healed, turn and face your wounds. Which is typically a threefold strategy: confront pain, process it, and reclaim your vitality and freedom.

Needless to say, these aren’t “three easy steps.” Setting your soul to rights isn’t for quick-fixers and resolution junkies. Deep old wounds, certainly traumas, are emotional superfund sites that aren’t going to be cleaned up overnight, or tidied up with a hankie and a good cry. Nor is breakthrough a one-and-done, an obstacle you leap over in a single bound.

It requires unflagging compassion and patience with yourself, a supportive community if not professional guidance, and a life stable enough to handle the confrontation. It typically starts when you reach a tipping point—when the fear of facing the truth is finally exceeded by the pain of not facing it, and you realize that something inside you needs to be admitted, in both senses of the word. Needs to be owned up to, and needs to be welcomed in, allowed into consciousness.

Source: Jarmoluk / Pixabay

And it requires understanding that though you crave closure—healing, restoration, finishing unfinished business, maybe even discovering the purpose for the pain—closure is more a verb than a noun. It can’t be forced, as hungry as you might be for emotional efficiency, to turn lemons into lemonade, and to make the past come to heel.

In fact, I’m not convinced you can completely heal a wound sustained 40 years ago with anything you do in the present, though I’ve certainly put my shoulder to that wheel on many occasions. The wound also belongs to its own time, is to some degree out of your reach, and the past is not always yours to project-manage. As the 12-steppers say, you’re always in recovery.

Still, in the present time, these old wounds, these things that weren’t your fault, tend to lodge themselves in the middle of your path, between your intentions and your achievements, between you and your aliveness, and you’ll constantly stumble there and not know why. Until you turn on the receiver. Until you realize that healing old wounds is like extracting a fishhook—you have to back it up a little before pulling it out.

item.title: Scheduling Time to Worry: How to Calm an Anxious Mind
item.description:
Anxiety

Scheduling Time to Worry: How to Calm an Anxious Mind

If you've laid awake at 2 a.m. worrying about the future, this is for you.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Left unchecked, worries can eat up large parts of the day—and get in the way of enjoying life.
  • Scheduling time to worry may feel counterintuitive, but this is a simple yet effective tool for coping.
  • To get started, set aside 15-20 minutes at the same time daily, and write out all your worries from the day.
  • This coping skill helps organize, contain, and make sense of unhelpful thoughts and worries.
Anxiety can feel uncomfortable and distressing, but it does not need to rule day-to-day life.
Source: Markus Winkler / Pexels

Your alarm goes off, but you have been awake for an hour already, fretting about the day—worrying about work meetings, climate change, and school pickup logistics.

As the day goes on, you find yourself in a constant state of anticipating, planning, dreading, and spiraling out about possible worst-case scenarios. You feel exhausted just by keeping up with your own thoughts.

Worry is a key symptom of generalized anxiety disorder, but you do not need to meet full criteria for this diagnosis to know how debilitating worry can be.

Thankfully, there are tools that can help. For example, worry time, outlined below, is a cognitive behavioral therapy intervention that involves setting aside a fixed amount of time daily to physically write out worries. Worry time has been shown to decrease the severity of worry, anxiety, negative affect, and insomnia (McGowan & Behar, 2012).

The Problem With Worry

For those prone to anxiety, worries may be a normal part of daily life. You may find yourself worrying about your children, aging parents, work, health, the state of the world, and that weird sound the car has been making… all before 8 a.m.

It may seem like just a few minutes here and there, but those minutes add up. Put together, you may be inadvertently worrying for hours a day at the expense of your well-being. Worries have a tendency to spiral endlessly, with no clear conclusion.

Worries also catapult us into the future and away from the present moment. In many ways, worrying is the opposite of mindfulness.

The Paradox of Scheduling Time to Worry

Scheduling worry time may seem like a paradox (who wants to worry?). One reason worry time is effective is that it consolidates worry into a confined time period, rather than letting unhelpful thoughts run rampant at all times of day or night.

It is also helpful to write out worries to create enough space to see them clearly for what they are: thoughts, not necessarily facts. Writing can feel cathartic, as it helps us identify, label, and process what is actually going on inside.

Seeing worries written out can also help shift the anxious mind from rumination to problem-solving or acceptance. Worry time helps us organize and focus our thoughts rather than letting them spin out of control.

Scheduling worry time also adds an element of certainty to an otherwise uncertain context. While worry time in itself cannot solve life stressors, having a routine, predictable aspect of your schedule can help release the grip that anxiety might have on you.

Instructions for Worry Time

  1. Set aside 15-20 minutes and put this on your calendar just as you would an appointment. Evening is an ideal time to schedule worry time as you can reflect on the day, but try to avoid doing this activity right before bed as it can be activating.
  2. When it is time to worry, grab a pen and paper. Set a timer for yourself. Write down the entirety of worries on your mind in any format that works for you (bullet points, lists, narrative style, etc). Get specific about your worries!
  3. When the timer goes off, stop writing. Take a few deep breaths to refocus back to the present moment.
  4. When worries pop up throughout the day or in the middle of the night, make a mental note to include this during worry time (or write a note for yourself), but do not indulge the worries further. You can do this by saying, “I’ll worry about this during worry time.”
  5. Repeat this exercise daily at the same time of day.

Conclusion

Worries can be an uncomfortable part of the human experience, but they do not have to dictate daily life. Scheduling worry time is a quick and effective tool for coping with anxiety. While this approach will not eliminate anxiety, containing worries to a predictable, short period of time each day can be a relief.

It may feel strange at first to invite worries in—especially if you’ve been stuck in an ongoing tug-of-war struggle against them. As with any new skill, consistency and practice are key. The more you use this approach, the more helpful it is likely to be.

For anxiety that continues to escalate to the point that it gets in the way of daily life, consider reaching out to a mental health professional for support.

item.title: 3 Strategies for Supporting Kids’ Mental Health Year-Round
item.description:
Parenting

3 Strategies for Supporting Kids’ Mental Health Year-Round

Parents can center routines around values that promote emotional well-being.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Parents set the tone, values, and routines that nurture kids' emotional well-being.
  • Interacting with nature increases focus, energy and positivity.
  • Parents can encourage digital-free hangout time and teach kids about boundary-setting with devices.
Source: Any Lane / Pexels

As a child therapist working with anxious and depressed kids, I know that back-to-school time brings up a lot for parents, kids, and families. New schools. Socializing and fitting into peer groups. Academic pressure. Physical appearance. Teasing and bullying.

All of this—and more—is a lot to navigate! But both parents and kids can get ahead of the school year’s stress pile-up by establishing healthy habits and routines at the outset that will positively shape kids’ mental health throughout the school year.

And best of all, the inspiration for these strategies comes from the summer camp playbook!

From new friendships to challenge courses to song circles around the campfire, kids thrive at camp. Time in nature with friends alongside a healthy dose of independence and creativity is just as exciting today as it was 30 years ago.

As summer winds down, school need not be a rough transition. Rather, it can be an opportunity for families to renegotiate household rhythms and reset family values.

Here are several basic ingredients that parents can translate into routines that guide family life and build long-term resilience.

1. Exposure to nature

A new global study adds to an already existing body of research demonstrating that when people spend time in or interact with nature in some way—anything from a walk in a park to looking out the window to watching a nature documentary or playing with a pet—they feel significantly better. Indeed, psychiatrists actually give out “park prescriptions” to kids whose depressed or anxious moods or ADHD benefits from playing outside in the fresh air. It’s cheap, it’s accessible, and it works quickly!

In the UK, community health practitioners are doing something similar with green social prescribing, or prescribing nature-based interventions like gardening or cycling to the same effect. In Japan, shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, has long been a popular medical and therapeutic intervention, as studies show that it lowers symptoms of depression and anxiety and boosts mood.

Here are some simple ways to integrate nature into weekly routines:

  • Kids can walk or bike to and from school and enjoy the benefits of fresh air, exercise, and nature.
  • Kids can play more outdoors in their parks or neighborhoods. If you’re concerned about safety, you can ask a responsible teenager to accompany them or rotate flexible parents.
  • Monthly/bimonthly/weekly family excursions. Draw from a hat: beach, lake, river, park, forest, hike, bike, swim, etc, or co-create a family bucket list of places to go or fun outdoor activities.
  • Does your child have reading homework? Encourage them to take it outside on a balcony, blanket in the grass, hammock, treehouse, park, etc.

2. Face-to-face socializing (that does not involve devices!)

Kids thrive on socializing, and it’s a key part of their growth and development. But not all socializing is created equal. Remember the last time that you walked past a group of kids clustered together, all staring at their individual phones? Or staring at one glowing screen altogether?

Yes, yes, parents often model this very same behavior. We also know how incredibly addictive screen time is (it literally alters dopamine like a drug). Studies consistently show that increased time spent on devices—particularly social media—makes kids feel more anxious and depressed. But kids benefit from adult guidance in setting limits and boundaries in the digital landscape.

Your kids may initially balk, but deep down, someday they will thank you if you set some parameters around their screen use. Some parents ask tweens to drop their smartwatches or phones into a basket when they come over to visit. Or you can set a household rule that when friends are over, devices are on sleep mode unless needed for something specific.

You can help brainstorm with your kids a “Screen-Free Stuff To Do List.” Perhaps this lives on your fridge so you don’t have to listen to a chorus of “I’m bored,” “there’s nothing to do,” “Can we please just watch/play/look at...?” Sometimes, kids just need a gentle reminder that so many other possibilities exist IRL to keep them from defaulting to a glowing screen.

3. Hands-on creativity

From lanyards to string bracelets to candle-making to jewelry to tie-dye T-shirts, creating with your hands is an unofficial summer camp motto. And kids love it. As an art therapist, I can attest that so much goodness happens when kids focus on creating with their hands: rumination decreases, repetitive movements soothe their nervous systems, glimmers of satisfaction and contentedness and even confidence register on their faces or elevate their moods. Sure, there are moments of frustration that can arise, but these are not the enemy. Frustration offers kids a chance to learn both how to problem-solve and how to persist.

Many parents have an art area or a messy kids' table in their homes. Or you can set up the kitchen table for specific projects. I always think it can be a double win if you have a table outside where kids can create in the open air.

When families make space to create together, perhaps as part of a weekly routine, that reminds kids that it’s an outlet and an alternative to screen headaches. Seasonal art-making is an annual reminder of pumpkin carving, costume design, wreath-making, cookie decorating, flower arranging, etc.

Some fun creative family-friendly projects:

  • Spice art: kids can spice up a bowl of water and then place a sheet of paper atop the water to absorb the design (e.g., turmeric, cinnamon, basil).
  • Simple monoprint: paint a leaf, or carve and paint a potato, then press onto paper. Repeat.
  • Hot glue nature sculptures: search for nature friends (flower petals, stones, bark, leaves) and then assemble sculptures with hot glue.
  • Eco-mobiles: use whatever materials you’ve got to create a hanging sculpture (save old tea bags, corks, bottle caps, gift wrap, etc.).
  • Collage: source scraps of paper, bags, magazines, or cards and glue onto paper (nice room decoration)!

Kids today face mounting pressures from many directions. In my office, I hear about so many layers of struggle on the micro and macro levels. As kids navigate the current maze of existential distress, they need more outlets that are tangible, at their fingertips, and allow for emotional release.

Picture letting go of a balloon that you just blew up and watching it deflate as it flies and hisses through the air. Our kids, like a balloon, inflate with daily pressures, and they need a release at the end of the day. Nature, socializing, and creativity are easily embedded into school-year routines and offer the space and permission for kids to blow off steam at the end of the day.

At any time, parents can plant and water these seeds to promote emotional well-being. Not only that, but they stand to benefit, too!

item.title: Cold Case Cleopatra
item.description:
Forensic Psychology

Cold Case Cleopatra

Exploring psychology and certainty in the forensic realm via Cleopatra's death

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Human intolerance for uncertainty often leads us to premature conclusions.
  • This tendency can be particularly damaging in the forensic realm.
  • We can see this highlighted in the infamous, and yet somewhat obscure, case of Pharaoh Cleopatra VII.
Source: Matthew Sharps

Human beings have a psychological need for certainty, for closure, that frequently outruns the evidence that would make such certainty reasonable.

This is a special problem in criminal justice. Hundreds of DNA-based exonerations show that juries frequently convict the wrong person, based on premature conclusions (Selby, 2025). In some societies, this need for “closure” can result in the deliberate conviction of a person completely innocent of the given crime, as an example of vicarious responsibility.

My own research (Sharps et al., 2013) has shown that in cases of especially vicious crime, people are more likely to hold the accused responsible than would be supported by the evidence, and are more likely to ignore evidentiary flaws in more violent crimes. Our human need for psychological closure is strong; this should not be ignored by anyone interested in impartial justice.

An excellent example can be found in one of the most infamous cold cases in history: the death of Cleopatra VII of Egypt.

Some of the details of the Pharaoh Queen’s career are universally acknowledged. Using a combination of sexuality and political acumen (modern scholars focus on her undoubted political skills), Cleopatra manipulated Julius Caesar into supporting her as sole ruler of Egypt. After Caesar’s assassination, she used her skills to ally with Marc Antony, a fine army officer but not the best naval officer in the world. When she believed she saw Antony defeated at the sea battle of Actium (31 BC), she sailed back to Alexandria with all speed. Antony, seeing her departure, abandoned his own fleet and chased after her, to his everlasting disgrace.

And now things got weird.

Antony’s enemy Octavian, the future Caesar Augustus, was certain to take revenge on Cleopatra. So, the story has always been that she locked herself in her tomb, had a venomous asp smuggled in past the guards, and let it bite her to death.

Suicide, before Octavian had a chance to grab her and parade her in chains before the Romans. Makes sense.

We will not embarrass specific scholars here; our interest is in the general psychology involved. But just as there are firm believers in the asp theory, there are equally firm believers that it’s complete nonsense. Scholars oppose each other on the asp theory with contrary and adamantine beliefs, but based on what?

Some ancient writers refer to an asp, or perhaps even two, but there are problems. For one thing, an asp bite, if it killed you, would take hours of agony to do so. Nobody in their right mind would select death by asp. On the one hand, Cleopatra was no herpetologist, but on the other hand, she was intelligent and well-educated—she would never have selected an asp. These are reasons anti-asp scholars, just as convinced as the snake fans, are certain that no asps were involved.

On another hand, however, most ancient writers weren’t herpetologists either—they may have confused asps with other snakes. Some pro-snake writers don’t even mention asps by name. It’s possible the snake was an Egyptian cobra, or maybe even something like an imported Russell’s Viper, a fabulously unpleasant animal with which I personally developed a nasty acquaintance (Carr et al., 1982). Maybe somebody even brought Cleopatra a fabulously toxic Mamba from sub-Saharan Africa.

Yet all of these snakes, except maybe the insanely venomous mamba, require many minutes or hours to kill you, and it’s difficult to imagine somebody stuffing six or eight feet of writhing mamba into a basket to smuggle into the Queen’s tomb. Some scholars extend this to the firm conclusion that no snake could have been involved, since it would have been writhing around in its basket, and guards would certainly have noticed this and prevented its being delivered to the Queen.

Yet I have personally seen a variety of venomous snakes, including the aforementioned rotten Russell’s Viper, lying perfectly quiescent in their transport baskets; anyone who knows snakes knows they are perfectly capable of immobility. However, many classical scholars have never worked in behavioral herpetology, so they are convinced that any given snake would be doing gymnastics in its basket all the same.

Cleopatra’s two servants were also killed with her, presumably by suicide, and there are scholars who hold that this completely disproves the snake theory. What snake has enough venom to take out three people, as well as that sort of work ethic? Yet there are many other suicidal possibilities; nothing mandates servant suicide by snake.

And there’s still another anti-snake faction, which holds with equal firmness that Cleopatra didn’t commit suicide at all. Octavian killed her.

When he’d already dragged her children through Rome, alive in chains, as trophies? When the last thing he would have wanted in an unsettled East was a royal Egyptian martyr? Octavian needed her alive, for the propaganda value if nothing else. But many scholars seem to have an idealized Cleopatra in mind, essentially a modern feminist on the lines of Star Wars’ Princess Leia, who would never have committed suicide, whatever the circumstances—certainly not over something as trivial as Antony or her own deposition.

Yet any psychologist in the forensic realm is aware of the profound irrationality that may be present in the minds of the suicidal, and of the extraordinarily dissociative processes that may lead to bizarre behaviors under those circumstances (Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026). For the competent forensic psychologist, any of the scenarios of Cleopatra’s death may conceivably have had some validity.

Despite the need for certainty on the part of scholars, especially those who keep turning up on TV, we just don’t know. We just don’t know about Cleopatra, or, for that matter, about Jack the Ripper, or the Hindenburg, or D.B. Cooper, or the many other conspiracy-laden or relatively obscure cases that keep cropping up.

If we wish to be forensically responsible, we must acknowledge that, psychologically, we don’t like uncertainty, but we must also sometimes accept uncertainty, in ancient cases and in our modern world.
